--- title: "Price & Performance" subtitle: "How horsepower, body style, and manufacturer positioning relate to MSRP" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(plotly) library(scales) msrp_df <- read_csv("data/processed/msrp_merged.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) recent_df <- read_csv("data/processed/recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) n_total_msrp <- nrow(msrp_df) n_mainstream <- sum(msrp_df$msrp <= 250000) n_exotic_outliers <- sum(msrp_df$msrp > 250000) n_recent_hp <- sum(!is.na(recent_df$horsepower_combined)) ``` ::: ## Overview & Available Performance Variables To test whether higher vehicle prices buy proportionally more engine performance—or whether buyers primarily pay for body style and brand prestige—we examine **9,762** deduplicated new-vehicle observations from [`msrp_merged.csv`](data/processed/msrp_merged.csv) alongside **7,397** recent **2022–2027** trims from [`recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv`](data/processed/recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv). - **Available variables used here:** `horsepower` (engine HP), `msrp` (sticker price in USD), `make` (manufacturer), `model`, `year`, and `body_group` (8 consolidated vehicle body styles). - **Why torque is omitted:** Inspection of all cleaned datasets confirmed that `torque` is **100% missing** (`0` non-NA values out of `7,397` rows) in Trimslate's public CSV export and is not recorded in either the MSRP dataset or EPA certification tables. Rather than imputing or fabricating values, we focus strictly on verified **horsepower** and **MSRP** records. --- ## 1. Horsepower vs. MSRP Grouped by Vehicle Body Style To compare the linear dollar-per-horsepower relationship across body styles without million-dollar hypercars compressing the vertical axis, the faceted chart below displays **9,602** vehicles priced at or below **`$250,000`** (`98.4%` of our `9,762` MSRP observations, excluding **160** ultra-exotic outliers up to `$2,065,902`). ::: {.plot-container} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Filter extreme >$250k supercar outliers so linear slopes within each body style are legible faceted_df <- msrp_df |> filter(msrp <= 250000) |> mutate( hover_text = paste0( "", year, " ", make, " ", model, "
", "Body Style: ", body_style, "
", "Horsepower: ", comma(horsepower), " hp
", "MSRP: ", dollar(msrp) ) ) p_body_scatter <- ggplot( faceted_df, aes(x = horsepower, y = msrp, color = body_group) ) + geom_point(aes(text = hover_text), alpha = 0.4, size = 1.3) + # Linear trend line per body style (inherit.aes = FALSE avoids hover text warnings) geom_smooth( aes(x = horsepower, y = msrp), method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#1b2838", linewidth = 0.7, inherit.aes = FALSE ) + facet_wrap(~ body_group, ncol = 4) + scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " hp")) + scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) + scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + labs( title = paste0( "Horsepower vs. MSRP Within Each Body Style (N = ", comma(n_mainstream), " Vehicles <= $250k)" ), x = "Engine Horsepower (hp)", y = "MSRP ($ Thousands)" ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "none") ggplotly(p_body_scatter, tooltip = "text") ``` ::: {#fig-hp-msrp-faceted .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: **Patterns & Findings:** Every body style exhibits a positive relationship between horsepower and MSRP, but the **price slope varies dramatically by segment**. **Coupes** and **Convertibles** climb steepest past `300 hp`—frequently crossing `$100,000–$250,000`—whereas **Pickups** and **Vans / Minivans** cluster tightly between `$20,000` and `$55,000` even when equipped with `300–400 hp` V6 and V8 towing engines. **Hatchbacks** occupy the most compact, budget-focused corner (`100–250 hp`, mostly under `$30,000`). --- ## 2. Horsepower per Dollar Across Manufacturers Which brands deliver the most raw engine output for your money, and which charge a luxury premium? Below, we calculate **horsepower per $1,000 of MSRP** (alongside exact **HP per $1** in the hover tooltip) across all **38 manufacturers** with at least 30 vehicles in our dataset (**`N = 9,681`** vehicles; `81` vehicles from `9` tiny boutique brands with `<30` models are excluded so small samples do not skew brand averages). ::: {.plot-container} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mfr_summary <- msrp_df |> mutate( hp_per_1k = horsepower / (msrp / 1000), hp_per_dollar = horsepower / msrp ) |> summarize( n_models = n(), mean_hp_per_1k = mean(hp_per_1k), mean_hp_per_dollar = mean(hp_per_dollar), mean_hp = mean(horsepower), mean_msrp = mean(msrp), .by = make ) |> filter(n_models >= 30) |> mutate( make = fct_reorder(make, mean_hp_per_1k), tier = case_when( mean_msrp >= 100000 ~ "Exotic / Ultra-Luxury (Mean MSRP >= $100k)", mean_msrp >= 40000 ~ "Luxury / Near-Luxury ($40k-$99k)", TRUE ~ "Mainstream (< $40k)" ), hover_text = paste0( "", make, " (n = ", comma(n_models), " vehicles)
", "Avg Value: ", round(mean_hp_per_1k, 2), " hp per $1,000 (", round(mean_hp_per_dollar, 4), " hp/$)
", "Avg Horsepower: ", round(mean_hp, 0), " hp
", "Avg MSRP: ", dollar(round(mean_msrp, 0)) ) ) n_mfr_vehicles <- sum(mfr_summary$n_models) p_mfr <- ggplot( mfr_summary, aes(x = mean_hp_per_1k, y = make, fill = tier, text = hover_text) ) + geom_col(width = 0.72) + scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " hp/$1k")) + scale_fill_manual( values = c( "Mainstream (< $40k)" = "#2b8cbe", "Luxury / Near-Luxury ($40k-$99k)" = "#7bccc4", "Exotic / Ultra-Luxury (Mean MSRP >= $100k)" = "#084081" ) ) + labs( title = paste0( "Average Horsepower per $1,000 of MSRP Across 38 Manufacturers (N = ", comma(n_mfr_vehicles), " Vehicles)" ), x = "Average Horsepower per $1,000 of MSRP", y = NULL, fill = "Market Segment" ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ggplotly(p_mfr, tooltip = "text") |> layout( legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.1), margin = list(b = 80) ) ``` ::: {#fig-hp-per-dollar-mfr .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: **Patterns & Findings:** Mainstream brands dominate raw horsepower-per-dollar value: **Dodge** leads all manufacturers at **`9.16 hp` per `$1,000`** (`0.0092 hp/$`, averaging `280 hp` at `$31,182`), followed by **Suzuki (`8.47`)**, **Pontiac (`8.45`)**, **Kia (`8.37`)**, **Chevrolet (`8.12`)**, and **Hyundai (`8.11`)**. Conversely, luxury and exotic badges sit at the bottom—**BMW (`5.44`)**, **Mercedes-Benz (`5.08`)**, **Porsche (`4.01`)**, **Ferrari (`2.23`)**, and **Rolls-Royce (`1.48 hp` per `$1,000`)**—demonstrating diminishing horsepower returns per dollar as buyers pay for craftsmanship, chassis engineering, and brand exclusivity. --- ## 3. Average MSRP Across Vehicle Body Styles Finally, we compare **average MSRP** across all eight consolidated body styles using the full **`N = 9,762`** dataset (including exotic models, while reporting **median MSRP** and the `<= $250k` trimmed average in each bar's tooltip to show the effect of high-end outliers). ::: {.plot-container} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} body_summary <- msrp_df |> summarize( n_vehicles = n(), mean_msrp = mean(msrp), median_msrp = median(msrp), trimmed_mean_msrp = mean(msrp[msrp <= 250000]), mean_hp = mean(horsepower), .by = body_group ) |> mutate( body_group = fct_reorder(body_group, mean_msrp), hover_text = paste0( "", body_group, " (n = ", comma(n_vehicles), " vehicles)
", "Average MSRP (all): ", dollar(round(mean_msrp, 0)), "
", "Median MSRP: ", dollar(round(median_msrp, 0)), "
", "Average MSRP (<= $250k): ", dollar(round(trimmed_mean_msrp, 0)), "
", "Average Horsepower: ", round(mean_hp, 0), " hp" ) ) p_body_msrp <- ggplot( body_summary, aes(x = mean_msrp, y = body_group, text = hover_text) ) + geom_col(fill = "#2c3e50", width = 0.68) + scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) + labs( title = paste0( "Average MSRP by Vehicle Body Style (N = ", comma(n_total_msrp), " Vehicles)" ), x = "Average MSRP (USD)", y = NULL ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ggplotly(p_body_msrp, tooltip = "text") ``` ::: {#fig-avg-msrp-body .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: **Patterns & Findings:** **Convertibles (`$96,084` mean; `$49,850` median)** and **Coupes (`$92,495` mean; `$46,150` median)** carry more than double the average MSRP of any other body style—partly because almost all six- and seven-figure supercars take two-door coupe or roadster form (even excluding `>$250k` exotics, Convertibles average `$72,145` and Coupes `$68,079`). Mainstream utility and family styles sit much closer to their medians: **Sedans (`$45,424` mean / `$32,970` median)**, **SUVs (`$41,313` mean / `$35,800` median)**, **Pickups (`$32,724`)**, **Vans / Minivans (`$30,603`)**, **Wagons (`$30,120`)**, and entry-level **Hatchbacks (`$23,364`)**. --- ## Limitations: Comparing 2001–2017 MSRP Data With 2022–2027 Vehicles Because our price analysis relies on [`msrp_merged.csv`](data/processed/msrp_merged.csv) (**2001–2017**) while our recent specification tabs use [`recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv`](data/processed/recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv) (**2022–2027**), three concrete limitations apply: 1. **Post-2017 price inflation is not captured in nominal MSRPs:** U.S. new-vehicle transaction and sticker prices rose substantially after 2020, so a `$33,050` median MSRP in our 2001–2017 data reflects earlier nominal dollars rather than 2022–2027 showroom stickers. 2. **Higher baseline horsepower in 2022–2027:** Across the **2,669** recent 2022–2027 trims with certified engine output, horsepower averages **330.2 hp** (median **305 hp**), up from **265 hp** (median **252 hp**) in our 2001–2017 MSRP dataset due to widespread turbocharging and larger SUV/truck lineups. 3. **Electrified powertrain gaps:** Modern battery-electric vehicles (EVs) and full hybrids—which play a major role in 2022–2027 pricing and acceleration—had minimal market share prior to 2017 and frequently lack combined system horsepower in EPA engine-certification tables. For those vehicles, we avoid merging incompatible years and instead examine recent powertrains directly on the **[Fuel Economy](fuel.qmd)** and **[Car Explorer](explorer.qmd)** pages.
